items.title: An Examination of Corporate Compliance Gaps in the Implementation of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
items.abstract: The Regulation on Artificial Intelligence, commonly known as the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, entered into force in August 2024 and has since been applying to companies in stages that stretch from February 2025 through December 2027 and beyond. This staggered timetable, compounded by a Digital Omnibus agreement that has already pushed back the deadline for full compliance with the rules governing stand-alone high-risk systems from August 2026 to December 2027, has left many companies uncertain about precisely what is required of them and by when. This article examines the compliance gaps that have opened between the obligations the Act imposes on providers, deployers, importers and distributors of artificial intelligence systems and what companies operating in or serving the European Union have actually implemented. Drawing on the regulatory text itself, recent readiness research indicating that a large majority of enterprises still lack a basic inventory of the artificial intelligence systems they use, and the professional and academic commentary that has followed the Act’s phased rollout, the article traces gaps across five domains, namely the identification and risk classification of artificial intelligence systems, data governance and algorithmic bias, documentation and traceability, human oversight and artificial intelligence literacy, and post-market monitoring. The article concludes with a set of recommendations organized around enterprise-wide risk mapping, contractual allocation of responsibility across the artificial intelligence supply chain, and integrated board-level governance, intended to help companies close the gap between what the Act requires and what most organizations have so far put in place.

items.title: Applications, advantages, and limitations of artificial intelligence in medical education assessment: a systematic review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being integrated into medical education, where assessments are high-stakes and intricately linked to clinical competence, professional judgment, and patient safety. Although several recent reviews have broadly explored the use of AI in medical education, a focused, methodologically transparent synthesis of AI applications in assessment and evaluation remains limited. This systematic review aimed to (i) identify and classify AI tools and methods used in medical education assessment; (ii) examine their advantages, limitations, and ethical implications; (iii) map AI use to established assessment frameworks (Assessment of Learning [AoL], Assessment for Learning [AfL], Assessment as Learning [AaL], validity, and reliability frameworks); and (iv) clarify the evolving role of medical educators. A systematic review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines [1]. Six electronic databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, ERIC, and Cochrane Library) were searched for English-language records published between January 2019 and February 2026. The search combined terms related to artificial intelligence, generative AI, machine learning, assessment, evaluation, and medical education. Two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts against pre-specified PICOS criteria. The methodological quality was appraised using the Medical Education Research Study Quality Instrument (MERSQI). The findings were thematically synthesized. After deduplication, 1,247 records were screened; 187 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 62 studies met the inclusion criteria. Six themes emerged: (i) AI-supported assessment tools and platforms; (ii) AI use across AoL, AfL, and AaL; (iii) validity, reliability, and feasibility considerations; (iv) medical-education–specific applications including written examinations, objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs – standardized, station-based assessments of clinical competence), simulation-based assessments, and workplace-based assessments (WBAs); (v) limitations including algorithmic bias, transparency, equity, and data privacy; and (vi) the redefined role of medical educators. The strength of the available evidence, judged descriptively on the basis of MERSQI scores, was variable: most studies were small-scale feasibility or proof-of-concept reports, and few were high-quality validation studies. AI has the potential to improve the efficiency, individualization, and timeliness of feedback in medical education assessment, particularly in large-scale written examinations, OSCE grading, and longitudinal competency tracking. However, evidence of improved validity or reliability is limited to narrowly bounded tasks, current evidence is heterogeneous and dominated by feasibility studies, and concerns regarding bias, transparency, equity, and the irreplaceable role of professional human judgment persist. AI should be positioned as a complement, not a substitute, for expert human evaluation. Medical educators, institutions, and regulators must develop validation, governance, and AI literacy frameworks before AI tools can be safely deployed in high-stakes assessments.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION, ADMINISTRATIVE INNOVATION AND ORGANISATIONAL EFFICIENCY IN SERVICE-BASED INDUSTRY, IMO STATE
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship among artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, administrative innovation and organisational efficiency in the service-based industry in Imo State, Nigeria. The study examined the effect of AI adoption on organisational efficiency, its effect on administrative innovation, and the mediating role of administrative innovation in the relationship between AI adoption and organisational efficiency. The study was anchored on the Technology-Organisation-Environment (TOE) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV). A cross-sectional survey design was adopted. The population comprised management and operational staff of service firms in banking, telecommunications, hospitality and health-service sub-sectors. Using the Taro Yamane formula, 320 respondents were selected through stratified random sampling, while 300 valid responses were obtained, representing a 93.75 per cent response rate. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients of 0.84, 0.81 and 0.86 for AI adoption, administrative innovation and organisational efficiency, respectively. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression and mediation analysis. Findings indicated high levels of AI adoption (mean = 3.94), administrative innovation (mean = 3.81) and organisational efficiency (mean = 3.88). AI adoption significantly affected organisational efficiency (β = 0.71, t = 12.84, p < 0.05) and administrative innovation (β = 0.68, t = 11.02, p < 0.05). Administrative innovation significantly mediated the relationship between AI adoption and organisational efficiency (β = 0.24, t = 5.16, p < 0.05). The study concluded that AI generates greater efficiency when supported by administrative restructuring and innovation. Service firms should therefore integrate AI adoption with workflow redesign, employee training and strategic administrative innovation, while government and regulators should provide supportive incentives and capacity-building programmes. Future studies should examine other sectors and states using longitudinal designs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Employment: Opportunities and Challenges for Youth
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important source of technological change in modern economies. Its development is influencing the way firms organise production, provide services and allocate tasks between workers and technology. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence and employment, with particular attention to young workers. It adopts a literature-based theoretical approach and discusses the potential employment opportunities and challenges associated with AI. Economic theories of technological change suggest that technology can substitute for labour in some tasks while complementing labour in others. AI may therefore reduce demand for certain routine tasks while increasing demand for workers with analytical, digital, creative and interpersonal capabilities. Recent international evidence also indicates that exposure to generative AI does not necessarily imply complete job replacement; in many occupations, the more likely effect is transformation of existing tasks. The paper discusses the possible effects of AI on labour demand, productivity, occupational change, skills and youth employment. It also highlights the importance of education, reskilling and lifelong learning in helping young people adapt to technological change. The paper concludes that the economic consequences of AI depend not only on the technology itself but also on how firms, educational institutions, governments and workers respond to the transition.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Components and Job Redesign in Nigerian Tertiary Institutions: Does Organizational Culture Matter
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into administrative work, yet evidence remains limited on whether specific AI components translate into measurable job redesign and whether organisational culture conditions this relationship. This study examined the relationships between optical character recognition (OCR), chatbots and virtual assistants (CVA), robotic process automation (RPA), organisational culture and job redesign. Objectives: To assess the associations of OCR, CVA and RPA with job redesign and determine whether organisational culture moderates these relationships among administrative personnel. Methods: A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted among 323 respondents. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, multiple linear regression, and hierarchical moderation regression were used. Statistical inference was based on regression coefficients, F tests, P values and explained variance. Results: Respondents reported relatively favourable levels of OCR (M = 3.882, SD = 0.831), CVA (M = 3.849, SD = 0.873), organisational culture (M = 3.819, SD = 0.849), RPA (M = 3.811, SD = 0.905) and job redesign (M = 3.730, SD = 0.868). Correlations among variables were minimal. Collectively, OCR, CVA, and RPA explained only 0.2% of variance in job redesign, and the regression model was not significant (F(3,319) = 0.165, P = 0.920). None of the predictors was independently significant: OCR (β = 0.014, P = 0.797), CVA (β = 0.021, P = 0.708), and RPA (β = 0.031, P = 0.582). Organisational culture did not significantly moderate the AI–job-redesign relationship (β = 0.018, P = 0.891). Conclusion: AI-component adoption was not associated with measurable job redesign in this sample, and organisational culture did not significantly alter these relationships. AI implementation may therefore enhance specific administrative processes without necessarily restructuring jobs. Recommendation: Institutions should complement AI deployment with task redesign, workflow integration, employee capability development and implementation-readiness strategies rather than assuming that technology adoption alone will transform jobs. Significant statement: These findings challenge a simple technology-deterministic assumption that AI adoption automatically produces job redesign and highlight the importance of examining the organisational and task-level mechanisms through which AI becomes consequential for work.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Dalam Sistem Peradilan: Kritik Hukum Progresif Terhadap Dehumanisasi Keadilan
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into judicial processes raises a fundamental question concerning the extent to which technological efficiency can be reconciled with the human-centred foundations of adjudication. This study critically examines the risk of the dehumanisation of justice arising from algorithmic decision-making and argues that the automation of adjudication cannot be assessed solely through the lens of procedural efficiency. Drawing upon Satjipto Rahardjo’s Progressive Law theory, the study investigates the normative tension between algorithmic rationality and the socio-legal dimensions of judicial reasoning, particularly judicial conscience, ethical discretion, and the capacity to depart from established legal patterns in pursuit of substantive justice. Employing normative legal research with philosophical and conceptual approaches, the analysis examines the limitations of AI-driven adjudication in relation to the human values underlying judicial decision-making. The findings demonstrate that, although AI can enhance procedural efficiency, consistency, and access to legal information, its reliance on historical data creates a structural risk of reproducing inherited biases and reinforcing mechanistic patterns of legal reasoning. More fundamentally, AI lacks the normative agency, moral consciousness, and ethical judgment required to undertake progressive legal interpretation when formal rules produce substantively unjust outcomes. The study therefore proposes a Human-in-the-Loop framework in which AI operates as a supporting instrument rather than an autonomous adjudicative authority, while final judicial determinations remain subject to meaningful human deliberation, ethical responsibility, and judicial discretion. The study contributes to the emerging scholarship on AI and law by introducing Progressive Law as an Indonesian jurisprudential framework for critically evaluating algorithmic adjudication. It further argues that the legitimacy of digital justice depends not merely on technological accuracy or efficiency, but on the preservation of human agency as an essential condition of substantive justice. Abstrak Meningkatnya integrasi kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dalam proses peradilan menimbulkan persoalan mendasar mengenai sejauh mana efisiensi teknologi dapat dipertemukan dengan fondasi kemanusiaan dalam proses ajudikasi. Penelitian ini secara kritis mengkaji risiko dehumanisasi keadilan yang muncul dari penggunaan pengambilan keputusan berbasis algoritma serta menegaskan bahwa otomatisasi peradilan tidak dapat dinilai semata-mata berdasarkan efisiensi prosedural. Dengan menggunakan teori Hukum Progresif Satjipto Rahardjo sebagai landasan analisis, penelitian ini mengkaji ketegangan normatif antara rasionalitas algoritmik dan dimensi sosio-legal dalam penalaran hukum, khususnya yang berkaitan dengan nurani hukum, diskresi etis, serta kemampuan hakim untuk menyimpangi pola hukum yang telah mapan demi mewujudkan keadilan substantif. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode penelitian hukum normatif dengan pendekatan filosofis dan konseptual untuk menganalisis keterbatasan ajudikasi berbasis AI dalam kaitannya dengan nilai-nilai kemanusiaan yang mendasari pengambilan keputusan yudisial. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa meskipun AI mampu meningkatkan efisiensi prosedural, konsistensi, dan akses terhadap informasi hukum, ketergantungannya pada data historis menimbulkan risiko struktural berupa reproduksi bias masa lalu dan penguatan pola penalaran hukum yang mekanistik. Lebih mendasar lagi, AI tidak memiliki agensi normatif, kesadaran moral, dan pertimbangan etis yang diperlukan untuk melakukan interpretasi hukum progresif ketika penerapan aturan formal berpotensi menghasilkan ketidakadilan substantif. Atas dasar tersebut, penelitian ini menawarkan kerangka Human-in-the-Loop, yang menempatkan AI sebagai instrumen pendukung dan bukan sebagai otoritas ajudikatif yang otonom, sementara penentuan putusan akhir tetap berada dalam proses deliberasi manusia yang bermakna, bertanggung jawab secara etis, dan berlandaskan diskresi yudisial. Kebaruan penelitian ini terletak pada penggunaan Hukum Progresif sebagai kerangka jurisprudensial Indonesia untuk mengkritisi perkembangan ajudikasi algoritmik. Penelitian ini menegaskan bahwa legitimasi peradilan digital tidak hanya ditentukan oleh akurasi dan efisiensi teknologi, tetapi juga oleh kemampuan sistem peradilan untuk mempertahankan agensi manusia sebagai unsur fundamental dalam mewujudkan keadilan substantif.

Artificial Intelligence in Education refers to the integration of AI technologies - to enhance teaching, personalize the student experience, optimize administration, and support decision-making. India the country with diverse crowd of students of different socio-economic background, demographic conditions, languages, emerging AI technology and tools is going to play crucial role in achieving the Sustainable Development Goal(SDG)-4 which aims to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all. This paper will describe how AI tools like Machine Learning & Adaptive Algorithms, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Predictive Analytics, Intelligent Tutoring system (ITS) can be use to enhance Class-room teaching, Evaluation, Research, Administration, Accreditation i.e teaching learning process in all and reaching out to unreached. The paper also discuss challenges posed due overreliance on AI and strategies to ensure ethical use of AI, particularly in education.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies of the twenty-first century, significantly influencing educational systems across the globe.Teacher education, particularly inclusive teacher education, is experiencing a paradigm shift through AI-enabled pedagogies, adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring, predictive analytics, and automated assessment.Inclusive teacher education aims to prepare teachers capable of addressing the diverse learning needs of students regardless of disability, gender, socioeconomic background, language, ethnicity, or geographical location.AI offers substantial opportunities to strengthen teacher preparation by providing personalized professional learning, enhancing accessibility, improving instructional decision-making, facilitating differentiated instruction, and supporting evidence-based classroom practices.However, the rapid integration of AI into teacher education also presents several ethical, technological, pedagogical, and policy-related challenges.Issues concerning algorithmic bias, privacy, digital inequality, transparency, teacher autonomy, and professional ethics require careful consideration to ensure that AI contributes to equitable and inclusive educational outcomes.This article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence in promoting inclusive teacher education.It discusses the conceptual foundations of AI and inclusive education, explores the opportunities AI presents for teacher preparation, analyses existing challenges, and identifies future directions for policy, research, and practice.Drawing upon recent international literature and policy frameworks, including UNESCO recommendations and Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education), the paper argues that AI should complement rather than replace human educators.Effective implementation depends on responsible governance, digital competency development, ethical AI frameworks, and institutional readiness.The study concludes that AI possesses immense potential to transform inclusive teacher education when integrated thoughtfully with pedagogical values, human rights principles, and equity-focused educational policies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in EFL Education: A Critical Review of Risks Based on the Four Dimensions of English Core Competencies in China
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative AI in language education brings benefits but also significant risks. Yet existing reviews largely address these risks within general education frameworks, lacking discipline specific analysis. This paper systematically examines AI risks in EFL education through China's four-dimensional English core competencies: language competence, cultural awareness, learning ability, and thinking quality. The analysis reveals four educational risk categories: imbalanced skill development and output homogenization in language competence; Western-centric biases and cultural recolonization risks in cultural awareness; undermined learner autonomy and self-regulation in learning ability; and inhibited critical thinking and creativity in thinking quality. By shifting from general educational ethics to EFL specific concerns, this paper offers a discipline sensitive framework for risk identification and a theoretical foundation for future empirical research.

items.title: Artificial intelligence self-efficacy among iranian medical sciences students: academic, behavioral, and socioeconomic correlates
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education. This study assessed AI self-efficacy and its associated factors among medical sciences students with prior self-reported AI use. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 550 students from Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Iran, were recruited using convenience sampling through an online questionnaire distributed via university social media channels and student networks. The questionnaire covered demographic, academic, socioeconomic, and digital media use characteristics, as well as the Persian version of the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES). Prior self-reported AI use was assessed using a Likert-scale item; students selecting “not at all” were excluded. Univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses were used to examine factors associated with AI self-efficacy. Results The mean AISES score was 69.80 ± 13.34 on a standardized 0–100 scale. Educational level was associated with AI self-efficacy, with bachelor’s (β = 15.34, 95% CI: 8.05–22.64), master’s/PhD (β = 12.63, 95% CI: 6.88–18.48), and professional-doctorate students (β = 18.63, 95% CI: 13.71–23.55) having higher scores than residents. Higher GPA (β = 3.62, 95% CI: 2.44–4.80) and employment (β = 5.25, 95% CI: 1.03–9.49) were also associated with higher AI self-efficacy. Compared with < 1 h/day, educational digital-media use of ≥ 3 h/day was associated with higher AI self-efficacy, whereas recreational use of ≥ 3 h/day was associated with lower scores. Age and gender were not independently associated with AI self-efficacy. Conclusions AI self-efficacy was associated with academic, socioeconomic, behavioral, and educational characteristics among medical sciences students. These cross-sectional associations do not establish causality; longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal direction.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, HUMAN DIPLOMACY: FINDING THE RIGHT BALANCE
items.abstract: This article examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in modern diplomacy and explores the boundary between AI assistance and human diplomatic authority. It discusses how AI can support diplomatic work through public opinion analysis, translation, information processing, crisis monitoring, early-warning systems, and negotiation preparation. At the same time, the article considers significant risks, including bias, inaccurate outputs, misinformation, cybersecurity threats, privacy concerns, and cultural and contextual misunderstanding. Drawing on examples and evaluations from the U.S. Department of State, UNESCO, the OECD, and the U.S. Advisory Commission on Public Diplomacy, the article argues that AI should strengthen rather than replace human decision-making. While AI can improve the speed and efficiency of analyzing information, political judgment, ethical responsibility, interpersonal understanding, and decisions involving significant human consequences should remain under human authority.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, the knowledge problem, and academic judgment: an Austrian perspective
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have renewed claims that university teaching and research can be largely automated. This article argues that such claims confuse information processing with judgment. Drawing on Hayek’s theory of dispersed and tacit knowledge, Huerta de Soto’s analysis of computation and entrepreneurial discovery, and the theory of judgment under Knightian uncertainty, it explains why greater computational capacity does not eliminate the knowledge problem. Contemporary AI can retrieve, recombine, and generate large volumes of context-sensitive information, while memory and retrieval mechanisms allow earlier interactions to shape later outputs. These capabilities expand the range of plausible explanations and possible courses of inquiry, but they do not provide a purpose-independent criterion for determining which interpretation is relevant, which assumptions are defensible, or which course of action should be pursued. The article applies this distinction to higher education. Artificial intelligence is likely to substitute for some standardized and information-intensive academic tasks, including routine content delivery, retrieval, and preliminary synthesis. At the same time, it increases the relative importance of judgment-intensive functions: diagnosing misunderstanding, selecting worthwhile research questions, evaluating methods and evidence, mentoring students, and assigning responsibility for scholarly claims. The argument is therefore not that every existing university practice will persist unchanged, but that artificial intelligence shifts the comparative advantage of professors and universities toward the cultivation, evaluation, and institutional coordination of judgment under uncertainty.

items.title: Availability of performance evidence of approved AI diagnostic software in pathology and hematology morphology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML)-based in vitro diagnostic software is increasingly authorized for clinical use in digital pathology and hematology morphology. However, it remains unclear how often performance evidence is publicly available. We performed a systematic landscape analysis identifying 77 CE-marked or FDA-authorized AI/ML-based IVD software devices from 29 manufacturers, including 68 digital pathology and 9 hematology morphology devices, identified through a multi-source search of FDA databases, EUDAMED, PubMed, Google Scholar, manufacturer portfolios, and clinical conference proceedings. Publicly available device-specific performance evidence was identified for 30 devices (39%), while 47 devices (61%) had no identified publicly available performance evidence. Evidence availability was higher among devices with dual EU and USA authorization than EU-only devices (8/8, 100% vs 22/69, 32%; p < 0.001), and among hematology morphology devices than digital pathology devices (7/9, 78% vs 23/68, 34%; p = 0.02). In total, 15 distinct performance metrics were reported, covering discrimination, agreement, correlation, and prognostic categories. However, their use varied across publications, limiting direct cross-device comparison. While performance evaluation results do not require publication, our findings indicate a gap between evidence availability and regulatory authorization, alongside heterogeneous use of metrics. These factors may undermine confidence in innovative medical devices and hinder informed clinical adoption.

items.title: Balancing AI-Driven Adaptation and Learner Self-Regulation: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Learning Outcomes in Generative AI-Supported Education
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a decline in learner autonomy. This conceptual paper aims to develop a pedagogical framework to balance AI-driven adaptation with learner self-regulation in GenAI-supported educational settings. The framework was constructed based on an integrative analytical review of recent literature in the fields of GenAI in education, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI hybrid regulation. The framework proposes the concept of "Balanced AI–Learner Regulation," which structures the relationship across three graduated levels: AI-led regulation, co-regulation, and learner-led regulation. It also proposes the principle of "Adaptive Fading of AI Support," based on providing support according to need and then gradually reducing it as the learner’s capacity for independent self-regulation grows. The paper’s primary contribution lies in shifting the focus from maximizing GenAI usage to designing a pedagogical balance that preserves autonomy, self-regulation, and critical thinking alongside the improvement of academic performance.

items.title: Better Savvy than Sorry: The requirements for AI Literacy in the EU AI Act
items.abstract: [Preprint chapter for an upcoming book organized by the KU Leuven Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)] Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are ever more embedded in our daily lives, shaping the way we learn, work, communicate, and access both public and private products and services. The integration of AI in information and communication technology is perceived as holding the potential to automate tasks and deal with information in a way that exceeds human capacity. However, the disruptive and pervasive deployment of AI systems in our society can profoundly influence the rule of law, democracy and the realization of human rights. In many situations, interacting with AI systems is no longer an individual choice, but rather a mandatory gateway to essential services such as education, social benefits or border control. Knowing, understanding, and having adequate skills to critically assess and use AI systems is, therefore, not only a personal, but a civic necessity. Recognizing this societal imperative, the AI Act explicitly acknowledges the importance of equipping citizens with the knowledge, understanding and skills to engage with AI systems in their daily lives and define clear obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems in its Article 4. In this chapter, we explore AI literacy as it is framed within the regulation, identify possible gaps and propose recommendations.

items.title: Better Savvy than Sorry: The requirements for AI Literacy in the EU AI Act
items.abstract: [Preprint chapter for an upcoming book organized by the KU Leuven Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)] Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are ever more embedded in our daily lives, shaping the way we learn, work, communicate, and access both public and private products and services. The integration of AI in information and communication technology is perceived as holding the potential to automate tasks and deal with information in a way that exceeds human capacity. However, the disruptive and pervasive deployment of AI systems in our society can profoundly influence the rule of law, democracy and the realization of human rights. In many situations, interacting with AI systems is no longer an individual choice, but rather a mandatory gateway to essential services such as education, social benefits or border control. Knowing, understanding, and having adequate skills to critically assess and use AI systems is, therefore, not only a personal, but a civic necessity. Recognizing this societal imperative, the AI Act explicitly acknowledges the importance of equipping citizens with the knowledge, understanding and skills to engage with AI systems in their daily lives and define clear obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems in its Article 4. In this chapter, we explore AI literacy as it is framed within the regulation, identify possible gaps and propose recommendations.

items.title: Beyond AI Literacy: Understanding Health Care Workforce AI Enablement in the Generative AI Era
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of generative AI is transforming health care delivery, education, administration, and research. In response, health care organizations have invested heavily in AI literacy initiatives and workforce development programs. Existing frameworks primarily focus on whether health care professionals understand AI and whether they can engage with AI effectively. However, health care practice increasingly reveals that individuals with similar levels of AI literacy and AI engagement often contribute very differently to AI-enabled work and organizational adoption. Some professionals primarily use AI to improve their own work, whereas others facilitate AI adoption, coordinate stakeholders, and integrate AI into routine practice. This observation suggests that current perspectives may overlook an important dimension of workforce AI enablement. In this Viewpoint, we argue that AI literacy and AI engagement alone provide an incomplete explanation of how health care organizations realize the benefits of AI. Drawing upon literature from AI literacy, fluency theory, human-AI interaction, innovation diffusion, implementation science, and health care workforce development, we propose the health care workforce AI enablement matrix (HWAEM). HWAEM conceptualizes workforce AI enablement through 2 complementary capabilities: AI fluency and AI harnessing. AI fluency refers to the capability to engage with AI effectively, appropriately, and responsibly across professional contexts, whereas AI harnessing refers to the capability to identify opportunities for AI-enabled improvement, mobilize stakeholders, facilitate adoption, and integrate AI into collective work practices. The interaction of these capabilities generates 4 workforce profiles: AI novices, AI practitioners, AI facilitators, and AI leaders. Through HWAEM, this Viewpoint argues that health care workforce AI enablement is better understood through the complementary capabilities of AI fluency and AI harnessing than through AI literacy and AI engagement alone. We illustrate how these profiles manifest in health care practice and discuss implications for workforce development and AI implementation. HWAEM offers a new perspective for understanding health care workforce preparedness in the generative AI era and provides a foundation for future empirical research.

items.title: Bridging Utility and Ethics: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of AI Tool Usage and Its Impact on Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The main objective of this study is to understand the role of AI tools in shaping students’ learning by analyzing how they use them, their perceived usefulness, and their views on academic integrity. The study evaluated the intersection of usage patterns and academic performance. Using a descriptive-correlational approach, data were collected from a purposive sample of 393 students at Centro Escolar University during the 2024-2025 academic year using a self-made questionnaire that underwent a reliability test. The study examines whether students’ opinions on AI’s usefulness align with actual improvements in critical thinking and academic success. Results from multiple regression show that regular AI use is a strong predictor of perceived learning effectiveness, explaining R2=0.33 of the variance (F=37.48, p=0.001), mostly by providing quick answers to assignments. However, AI usage patterns only account for 8% of the variance regarding the perceived limits on critical thinking skills. The perceived threat to critical thinking comes from a reliance on AI due to time pressure. Ethically, there is a significant correlation between over-reliance and worries about academic integrity. The study recommends that universities implement process-based assessments, establish clear AI usage guidelines, and provide time-management support to reduce over-reliance while fostering independent analytical skills. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd), Academic Integrity, Student Learning Outcomes, Critical Thinking, Educational Technology.

items.title: ChatGPT and AI Tools in ESL/EFL Writing Instruction
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly OpenAI's ChatGPT, has transformedpedagogical paradigms across global higher education, presenting both innovative opportunities and complexchallenges for English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction.This systematic literature review synthesizes contemporary peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and2026 to critically examine the pedagogical benefits, ethical dilemmas, and instructional challenges associated withintegrating GenAI tools into L2 writing contexts. Following the PRISMA framework, a rigorous screening of academicdatabases (Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus) yielded 25 high-quality empirical and theoretical studies. Findingsindicate that GenAI functions as an effective cognitive partner, providing immediate formative feedback, expandingacademic vocabulary, lowering writing anxiety, and facilitating pre-writing brainstorming (Alsaedi, 2024; Deep et al.,2025). Conversely, the unguided adoption of AI writing assistants induces severe risks, including academicdishonesty, automated plagiarism, student cognitive atrophy, over-reliance, and the invalidation of traditionalproduct-based writing assessments (Perkins, 2023; Su & Yang, 2025). To address these tensions, the review outlinesstrategic pedagogical implications, recommending a shift toward process-oriented writing assessments, thecultivation of student and teacher AI literacy, and the formulation of ethical prompt engineering practices. Finally,future research directions are identified, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies on L2 language retention andcross-cultural comparisons of AI policies in tertiary education.

items.title: Cognitive Exoskeletons: Reconstructing Human Agency and Epistemic Pruning in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: This paper introduces the framework of the Cognitive Exoskeleton (인지적 외골격 체계) to redefine human epistemic agency in the era of advanced artificial intelligence. Conventional perspectives oscillate between techno-dystopian anxieties regarding intellectual atrophy and naive instrumentalism that reduces AI to a mere conversational search engine. Extending Andy Clark and David Chalmers’ Extended Mind Thesis, we argue that artificial intelligence functions not as an external substitute for thought, but as an intellectual exoskeleton. Just as heavy industrial machinery augmented somatic labor by overcoming biological physical constraints, algorithmic models liberate human cognition from biological computational bottlenecks—specifically exhaustive verification and computational recall. In this symbiotic paradigm, the primary role of human intellect shifts from memorization and brute-force computation to bold hypothesis generation and normative value alignment, utilizing machines as engines of hyper-velocity via negativa (algorithmic pruning of falsehoods).

items.title: Cognitive Outsourcing in Digital-Intelligent Education: Hidden Educational Risks and Regulatory Paths
items.abstract: The deep integration of artificial intelligence in classroom teaching reorganises learners' internal cognition and technologically mediated external cognition through the mechanism of cognitive offloading, fundamentally reshaping how knowledge is accessed and thinking is processed. Yet algorithmic limitations and misaligned learner orientations are driving this offloading toward risks of hollowed classroom interaction, flattened cognitive depth, and distorted feedback. This study systematically classifies these risks to fill a critical gap. Based on a four-dimensional framework of thinking, subject, knowledge, and practice, the risks are categorised as follows: at the thinking dimension, algorithmic opacity and data bias reduce instruction from thinking cultivation to answer retrieval, obstructing higher-order goals through a black-box trap that masks reasoning processes; at the subject dimension, the quasi-subjectivity of intelligent systems encroaches upon the learner's agency, triggering subject alienation and hollowing out authentic classroom interaction; at the knowledge dimension, fragmented algorithmic outputs are mistaken for systematic understanding, leaving comprehension at a superficial level; at the practice dimension, instant system responsiveness dissolves productive ambiguity and interrupts situated practical activities, disrupting human-machine synergy in situated learning. Through analysing these risks, this study proposes mitigation strategies across teaching, learning, and assessment: rebuilding classroom thinking space through generative dialogue between teachers and students; requiring independent learner reasoning before critical scrutiny of algorithmic outputs; and establishing a process-trace-centred evaluation mechanism that values drafts and revision histories to reflect genuine thinking development.

items.title: Continuity Without Certainty
items.abstract: Persistent human-AI systems can retain interaction history without treating it as an authoritative account of a person’s current needs. This paper develops revisable recognition as a behavioral model that keeps prior events, provisional beliefs, action-relevant uncertainty, initiative, and repair distinct. It connects AREN’s account of historical defeasibility and reciprocal interpretive influence to a program of evaluation. As an initial methods check, we ran a prompt-level benchmark of 36 model outputs across 12 restorative-space scenarios and three response conditions. Across 15 predesignated preference-change, scope, and correction opportunities, no response overtly enacted a superseded preference, although one output misrepresented the scope of a desk-specific restriction. All nine designated ambiguity responses named the unresolved choice. Two clear mirror requests drew unnecessary clarification, and a material-choice case could not be scored because the task card omitted the trade-off values it was said to contain. The benchmark had no human participants, no recorded model version or generation settings, and one coder who knew the conditions. These results test the prompts and codebook only; they do not establish condition effectiveness, persistent memory, or human experience.

items.title: Crisis-induced hybrid learning, cognitive offloading, and generative AI reliance among Pakistani CS undergraduates
items.abstract: Purpose In spring 2026, geopolitical tensions prompted the Pakistani government to mandate full online instruction (10 March–3 April 2026), followed by a hybrid schedule for the rest of the semester. This shift is treated here as an externally imposed crisis context for AI adoption, not as a natural experiment. No pre-crisis baseline or control group was available. The study characterises generative AI (GenAI) adoption patterns and the psychological antecedents of AI dependency among undergraduate computer-science (CS) students during this window. Three hypotheses, grounded in the reviewed literature, structured the analysis. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey was administered across Pakistani higher education institutions (HEIs) in April–May 2026. Of 360 responses collected, two incomplete records were removed, and a thirteen-criterion data-quality screen was ap-plied, yielding N = 299. Fourteen constructs were operationalised from UTAUT, Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS). Block-entry OLS regression and bootstrapped mediation (5,000 resamples) tested the hypotheses; ANOVA and Spearman correlations supported descriptive analysis of adoption patterns. Findings Adoption was near-universal (>99%), with 45.2% of respondents reporting ≥ 31% of submitted work directly AI-generated. A three-block OLS regression explained 54.6% of variance in AI dependency. Cognitive offloading was the strongest predictor (β = 0.41, p < 0.001), followed by procrastination (β = 0.23, p < 0.001), extrinsic motivation (β = 0.17, p = 0.002), and intrinsic motivation as a protective factor (β = −0.13, p = 0.013). Bootstrapped mediation confirmed procrastination partially mediates the extrinsic motivation–dependency path (ab = 0.201, 95% BC-CI [0.122, 0.289]). Originality/value To our knowledge, this is among the first studies to survey GenAI dependency during an active government-mandated crisis disruption in South Asian higher education. Contributions include a multi-theory construct battery adapted for a crisis context, a thirteen-criterion response-quality protocol, and evidence that habituated cognitive offloading and extrinsic motivation are the primary drivers of AI dependency in this context.

items.title: Cyber Security Awareness and Responsible AI Adoption: A Mediation Analysis of AI Risk Perception
items.abstract: Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into organisational workflows has introduced unprecedented cybersecurity challenges, necessitating a deeper understanding of how users perceive and respond to AI-related risks. This study investigates the mediating role of AI Risk Perception in the relationship between Cyber Security Awareness and Secure AI Usage Behaviour. Drawing on Protection Motivation Theory and employing a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 300 respondents across diverse industries using a structured questionnaire measuring three latent constructs. Mediation analysis, conducted using the PROCESS macro with bootstrap confidence intervals, revealed that Cyber Security Awareness has a strong positive effect on AI Risk Perception (path a: β = 0.712, p < 0.001), which in turn positively influences Secure AI Usage Behaviour (path b: β = 0.444, p < 0.001). The direct effect of Cyber Security Awareness on Secure AI Usage Behaviour remained significant (path c′: β = 0.413, p < 0.001), while the indirect effect through AI Risk Perception was also significant (β = 0.316, 95% CI [0.229, 0.404]). These findings support partial mediation, indicating that AI Risk Perception accounts for approximately 43.3% of the total effect. The results underscore the importance of integrating cybersecurity education with AI risk awareness programmes to foster responsible AI adoption.

items.title: Daily job crafting with generative artificial intelligence: Implications for work meaningfulness and engagement
items.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) becomes embedded in daily work, understanding how employees proactively engage with these tools to shape their work experiences is increasingly important. Building on self-determination theory and the job crafting literature, this study introduces the concept of daily Gen-AI-driven job crafting: employees' self-initiated use of Gen-AI to modify their daily job demands and resources. We examine whether Gen-AI-driven job crafting is associated with daily work engagement through psychological need satisfaction and work meaningfulness. We employed a daily diary design with 149 UK-based full-time employees (M age = 36.7, SD age = 10.4; 63.8% male) who used Gen-AI at work daily or multiple times per day over ten consecutive workdays, incorporating a brief open-ended question to examine whether employees experienced their Gen-AI use as intentional work modification. Quantitative results showed that the dimensions of Gen-AI-driven job crafting (augmenting instrumental resources, augmenting social resources, augmenting challenging demands, and automating hindering demands) were differentially associated with daily work engagement through need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and, in turn, work meaningfulness: the competence pathway received the most consistent support, while the relatedness pathway was the most limited. Open-ended responses were consistent with intentional work modification, for instance, automating hindering demands was framed as a strategic reallocation of cognitive resources toward more valued work rather than simple workload reduction. Together, these findings suggest that Gen-AI may function as a bottom-up work design tool associated with daily need satisfaction and engagement.

items.title: Defense-in-Depth for LLMs: Evaluating Memory Gates Against Activation-Induced and Memory-Induced Sycophancy
items.abstract: Long-term memory allows Large Language Models (LLMs) to maintain personalized context across interactions, but retrieved user history can induce memory-induced sycophancy, causing models to favor stored user beliefs over objective evidence. Existing defenses primarily operate on retrieved context and are rarely evaluated jointly with internal behavioral bias. We introduce a $2 \times 2$ defense-in-depth framework separating internal activation steering from external memory handling. We extract sycophancy steering directions from 100 paired prompts and evaluate four open-weight models across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on MemSyco-Bench (answers for all 1,550 items; defense conditions judged on a fixed 250-item subsample), with three LLM judges. Three of the five configurations are new (rewriting every memory, a Router Gate that keeps, rewrites, or drops each memory, and dropping all memory); the other two are MemSyco's baselines. Selective Router Gate filtering preserves substantially more of MemSyco's average accuracy than complete memory removal, and this separation persists when the models are steered toward sycophancy. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering ($α= -1.5$) lowers judge-averaged sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while average accuracy moves from 43.99% to 43.31%; this reduction has the same direction under all three judges but is not statistically significant (paired $p = 0.08$ to $0.63$ on 149 items). External memory filtering is the part of the design that holds up; our data do not show that inverse steering adds to it.

items.title: Designing for Organisational Capability: From Intended Outcomes to Sustained Performance
items.abstract: Why can an organisation invest in people, learning and technology, meet its performance targets, and still depend on particular individuals to keep work moving? Successful outcomes can conceal missing information, unclear decision authority and disconnected processes when capable employees compensate for weaknesses in the arrangements surrounding their work. Designing for Organisational Capability: From Intended Outcomes to Sustained Performance examines how organisations can deliberately design the conditions through which required outcomes are produced, sustained and adapted. Building on From Workforce to Organisational Capability, it develops an outcome-first approach that connects people, work, information, authority, learning, support and technology around the performance the organisation needs to achieve. A continuing illustrative service-team case carries the argument from defining the intended outcome to tracing work, strengthening interfaces and creating the conditions for workplace application. The paper then examines the relationship between human judgement and AI, how evidence makes performance evident, and how organisations build the capacity to adapt as operating conditions change. The discussion draws on research into training transfer, informal learning, organisational design, generative AI and dynamic capabilities, alongside NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework. It distinguishes these research foundations from the Capability Design applications developed within the paper. Written for leaders, learning and development professionals, work designers and organisational practitioners, the whitepaper offers a basis for examining whether investments have established dependable capability and what must work together for intended outcomes to become sustained performance. Part of the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series.

items.title: Digital Exaptation: The Evolutionary Mechanism of Emergent Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes the theory of Digital Exaptation (디지털 굴절적응) to resolve the foundational debate surrounding emergent reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Contemporary artificial intelligence discourse often views higher-order reasoning either as an unpredictable artifact of empirical scaling laws or dismisses it as mere statistical mimicry ("stochastic parrot"). Borrowing from evolutionary biologist Stephen Jay Gould’s concept of exaptation—wherein a trait evolved for one primary adaptive function is co-opted for an entirely novel utility (e.g., feathers evolving for thermoregulation before being exapted for aerodynamic flight)—we argue that reasoning in foundation models is not a teleologically designed objective, but an exaptive structural byproduct of hyper-dimensional statistical compression. By reframing LLM emergence through evolutionary biology, this paper bridges empirical machine learning and the philosophy of mind.

items.title: Disclosure willingness anthropomorphism and thinking style shape perceived fit and comfort in AI mental health chatbot interactions
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) conversational agents are increasingly used for everyday, non-clinical mental-health support, yet little is known about when these exchanges feel fitting and comfortable. We used a laboratory mixed-methods design to examine associations among perceived convenience of interaction (PCI), relational attitude (RA), willingness to self-disclose (WSD), anthropomorphism (AN), perceived fit/comfort (FC), and thinking style in 83 participants (43 rational-dominant; 40 experiential-dominant). WSD showed the strongest unique association with FC. A post hoc reverse model also found a unique FC-WSD association, leaving their temporal order unresolved. AN had no stable direct association with FC, but the WSD-FC association became stronger as AN increased. Group comparisons and continuous Rational-Experiential Inventory (REI) analyses converged: relatively stronger experiential processing was associated with higher AN, whereas relatively stronger rational processing was associated with higher WSD. The group-blind thematic analysis linked disclosure decisions to privacy, control, social distance, functional usefulness, and affective comfort. Together, the findings identify WSD as a key correlate of FC and show that anthropomorphism conditions this association rather than simply improving the interaction. Clear boundaries, controllability, and adjustable relational cues therefore warrant attention in future design research.

items.title: EFFECT OF AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE LEARNING PLATFORM ON SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS' RETENTION IN CHEMISTRY IN ANAMBRA STATE
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the effect of an Artificial Intelligence-Driven Adaptive Learning Platform (AI-DALP) on secondary school students’ retention in Chemistry within the Onitsha Education Zone of Anambra State, Nigeria. The study specifically assessed the difference in delayed retention between students taught using AI-DALP and those taught using the Conventional Teaching Method (CTM) after controlling for immediate posttest performance, as well as whether retention differed by gender within the adaptive learning environment. Guided by two research questions and two null hypotheses tested at the 0.05 level of significance, the study adopted a quasi-experimental non-randomised pretest–posttest control-group design. The population comprised 548 Senior Secondary School II (SS2) Chemistry students across 22 public co-educational schools. Through purposive sampling based on ICT infrastructure availability, a sample of 59 students (30 in the AI-DALP group and 29 in the CTM group) was selected. The intervention lasted six weeks, covering Oxygen, Hydrogen, and Halogens, followed by a delayed retention test administered two weeks after the posttest. Data were collected using a 50-item Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT), validated by three experts, with an internal consistency reliability coefficient of 0.82 established using the Kuder–Richardson 20 (KR-20) formula. Data were analyzed using mean, standard deviation, and Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) with posttest scores as the covariate. The results indicated that students exposed to AI-DALP achieved significantly higher adjusted retention mean scores than those taught via CTM after controlling for posttest performance. Additionally, no statistically significant difference was observed in retention scores between male and female students taught using AI-DALP after accounting for posttest performance. The study concluded that AI-DALP effectively enhances durable Chemistry learning among secondary school students regardless of gender. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Adaptive Learning, Chemistry Education, Delayed Retention, Secondary Education, Gender, Onitsha Education Zone.

items.abstract: Background: Clinical deterioration in hospitalized patients often precedes adverse events such as cardiac arrest, unplanned intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and mortality. While traditional early warning systems (EWS) based on vital signs have improved detection, their predictive accuracy and integration into nursing workflow remain suboptimal. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven systems leveraging nursing surveillance data may enhance early detection and response. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of an AI-driven early warning system integrated into nursing practice on early detection of clinical deterioration, nursing response time, and patient safety outcomes in adult medical-surgical wards. Methods: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial conducted across 12 medical-surgical units in two tertiary hospitals. Adult patients (N=4,286) were randomized to either the AI-driven EWS (intervention, n=2,143) or standard EWS care (control, n=2,143). The AI system analyzed nursing documentation patterns and vital signs in real time, generating risk scores displayed within the electronic health record. Primary outcomes included time to clinical deterioration detection, nursing response time to alerts, and composite patient safety outcomes (in-hospital mortality, unplanned ICU transfer, and cardiac arrest). Data were analyzed using intention-to-treat principles with mixed-effects models. Results: The AI-driven EWS significantly reduced time to deterioration detection (median 2.1 vs. 4.8 hours; p<0.001) and nursing response time (median 18 vs. 42 minutes; p < 0.001). The composite patient safety outcome occurred in 11.2% of intervention patients versus 16.8% of controls (adjusted odds ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.53-0.78; p<0.001). Unplanned ICU transfers were higher in the intervention group (24.9% increase; p=0.001), suggesting appropriate escalation. Conclusion: AI-driven EWS integrated into nursing practice substantially improved early detection, response time, and patient safety outcomes. These findings support implementation of AI-enhanced surveillance systems in acute care settings.

items.title: Effects of a self-regulated learning training on adolescents’ metacognitive awareness, learning processes and outcomes: a multi-method perspective
items.abstract: Abstract Adolescence represents an important developmental phase for self-regulated learning (SRL), marked by uneven growth in metacognitive knowledge, awareness, and regulatory skills. Research on supporting adolescents’ emerging SRL is particularly relevant in online learning environments (OLEs), where autonomous regulation is essential, but remains limited. This quasi-experimental field study examined immediate effects of a brief digital SRL training on secondary school students’ metacognitive awareness, learning outcomes, and regulatory processes during an online essay-writing task. The experimental group (EG; n = 37) received SRL training before the task, while a control group (CG; n = 32) received comparable training on ergonomics. Results showed significantly higher metacognitive awareness in the EG, but no effects on essay performance, domain-knowledge gains, or learning transfer. Process analyses revealed that the EG spent more time on task orientation, and prior domain knowledge (PK) moderated training effects on cognitive processes; in the EG, rereading and writing frequencies decreased with increasing PK, whereas they showed slight increases in the CG. Within-group associations showed more consistent positive links between PK and learning outcomes in the EG. Sequence analyses further suggested that successful EG students with different PK levels followed partly distinct regulatory pathways: high-PK students displayed metacognitive process sequences, whereas low-PK students relied more on planning-intensive mixed sequences. Overall, findings suggest that a brief SRL training can foster metacognitive awareness and selected regulatory behaviors, while highlighting the need for adaptive and temporally sensitive SRL support for adolescent learners. The study demonstrates the value of multi-method, process-oriented perspectives for informing future SRL intervention designs.

items.title: Effects of generative AI and translanguaging on second language writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency
items.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) exhibits the potential to scaffold L2 students’ writing, research found that L2 students struggle to craft effective prompts for GenAI to produce high-quality feedback and responses. As such, there is a need to incorporate translanguaging into L2 students’ prompt engineering to capitalize on the learning potential of GenAI for L2 students. The present study, therefore, investigated whether the combined use of GenAI and translanguaging influenced L2 writing linguistic features. We adopted a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental design by assigning L2 writers to four groups: a control group, translanguaging - only, GenAI - only, and translanguaging + GenAI. Comparing the lexical complexity, syntactic complexity, accuracy, and fluency of the four groups, we found that GenAI had a significant positive impact on the lexical and syntactic complexity, accuracy, and fluency of L2 students’ writing, while translanguaging alone and the combination of GenAI and translanguaging did not yield significant positive impacts on most indices of the writing performance. L2 teachers are encouraged to integrate GenAI tools into writing instruction to improve students’ writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency, while providing scaffolding for translanguaging, as its benefits might not emerge automatically, particularly for advanced L2 writers.

items.title: Effects of Visual-Proprioceptive Integration of Hand Position on Immersive Experience and Performance
items.abstract: We investigated how visual–proprioceptive conflicts regarding perceived hand position alter sense of embodiment and our actions during head-mounted display (HMD) virtual reality (VR). Participants hit virtual objects with virtual mallets (training phase) while we manipulated the amount and type of virtual hand offset, the visibility of virtual hands, and the presence of vibration cues. The manipulations differentially affected reported presence, perceived body ownership, and sense of agency. To examine the aftereffects of this training, participants were subsequently asked to strike a stationary virtual target without any visual representation of virtual hands or mallets. Hand offset during training biased the direction, and increased the variability, of these test strikes. A follow-up extinction experiment found little sign of attenuation across five consecutive strikes. These findings suggest brief exposures to visual–proprioceptive conflicts can bias perception and action beyond the immediate training context.

items.title: Efficacy and Mechanism of Generative AI in Empowering English Writing Instruction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence technology brings new transformative opportunities to English writing instruction. This paper analyzes the efficacy and mechanism of generative AI in empowering English writing teaching. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and Self-Regulated Learning theory, it summarizes teaching efficacy from three dimensions—the quality of writing output, cognitive support during the writing process, and real-time adaptation of writing feedback—and further reveals the underlying mechanism through three layers: cognitive load reduction, learning motivation activation, and metacognitive strategy activation. Using data from a 12-week quasi-experimental study, it compares the experimental and control groups in terms of writing performance, writing strategy use, and feedback engagement. The results show that generative AI-assisted instruction has a moderately strong facilitative effect on learners' writing performance, achieved mainly by reducing extraneous cognitive load, enhancing writing self-efficacy, and deepening feedback engagement. This study provides theoretical grounding and practical reference for integrating generative AI into the English writing classroom.

items.title: Embodied Education and Artificial Intelligence: an integrated pedagogical model for the design of hybrid, inclusive and reflective learning environments in secondary schools
items.abstract: This study analyses the integration of the embodied approach and artificial intelligence in educational contexts, investigating their effects on engagement, intrinsic motivation and school inclusion. The research, conducted at two upper secondary schools in the city of Naples, involved 180 students divided into an experimental group and a control group according to a quasi-experimental design. The experimental group took part in an 8-week educational intervention based on embodied activities, collaborative practices and guided use of generative artificial intelligence tools, whilst the control group followed traditional teaching activities. The study adopted a mixed-methods approach, integrating the Student Engagement Scale (SES), the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), semi-structured interviews and classroom observations. The results highlight a significant increase in engagement and intrinsic motivation within the experimental group, with preliminary positive indications also regarding the participation of students with special educational needs. The qualitative analysis further shows that AI-supported embodied activities fostered active participation, collaboration, multimodal accessibility and metacognitive reflection. Overall, the study suggests that the integration of embodied education and artificial intelligence, when supported by intentional pedagogical design, can contribute to the creation of more inclusive, reflective and participatory learning environments.

items.title: Empowering student-led climate solutions: the role of AI in STEAM education
items.abstract: This convergent mixed-methods study investigates the strategic integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into a university-level STEAM curriculum to empower students to design climate solutions. Combining quantitative survey data from 69 undergraduate students selected via a complete cohort census sampling approach (response rate: 84.1%) and multi-tiered purposive qualitative interviews with N = 25 participants ( N = 11 experts, N = 9 faculty members, and N = 5 student innovators), the findings indicate high technological familiarity and widespread adoption (100% AI tool use). Specifically, students reported the highest agreement for AI enhancing their creativity and learning independence (86.9%, M = 4.12), supporting their capacity to pivot from data collection to strategic solution design (73.9%, M = 3.78), and bolstering their perceived empowerment to propose climate solutions (76.8%, M = 3.84). Furthermore, self-reported student perceptions indicated that AI supported their critical thinking process (68.1%, M = 3.65), representing perceived cognitive scaffolding rather than an objective measure of skill performance. This supports the qualitative finding that AI acts as a “Complexity Mediator” in climate tasks. However, notable concerns were reported regarding accuracy (60.9%) and plagiarism (59.4%). To address this, the study proposes the AI-Empowered STEAM Climate Action Model (AISC-AM), a conceptual framework that structures STEAM as a Multi-Scalar Problem-Solving Ecosystem and mandates critical AI literacy and an “AI-in-the-Loop” validation structure. Informed by preliminary stakeholder appraisal, the proposed AISC-AM offers a structured pedagogical workflow to mitigate operational risks while connecting student-led research to regional climate policy platforms via youth organizational partnerships.

items.title: Ethnic Diversity, Organizational Diversity Climate, and the Perceived Value of Deepfake Personas: A User Study with Marketing Professionals
items.abstract: Beyond fraud, deepfake personas can be utilized in human-centered design to represent user groups. This study investigates how deepfake persona sets of different ethnic diversity can offer strategic value for human-computer interaction (HCI) design processes. In an online experiment with 81 marketing professionals evaluating persona sets of varying diversity, the more diverse sets were perceived as significantly more inclusive, more inspiring for market coverage, and more valuable for identifying market opportunities, with no compromise of perceived persona quality or task performance. Findings show that these perceived strategic benefits were consistently associated with organizational diversity climate, consistent with institutional theory. These findings advance persona, advertising, and HCI research by repositioning deepfake technology from a solely technological risk to a strategic design resource driven by the organizational diversity climate, with direct implications for inclusive HCI practice and diversity policies.

items.title: Examining the role of a structured AI-supported intervention in developing EFL students’ academic writing skills in Mozambican higher education
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping educational practices and redefining how academic writing is taught, learned, and assessed. This study explores the role of a structured AI-supported writing intervention on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students’ academic writing performance and examines lecturers’ awareness of, and alignment with, emerging AI trends in a Mozambican public university. Employing an Exploratory Sequential Case Study-Mixed Methods design, data were collected through documents analyses, interviews, an intervention, and observations. Participants included eighteen undergraduate EFL students and five lecturers. Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Social Practice Theory (SPT), qualitative data were analysed thematically, while quantitative data were examined using descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test to measure performance differences. Findings revealed that students in the control group had limited informal exposure to AI and lacked ethical guidance, whereas students participating in the structured AI-supported intervention demonstrated higher levels of academic writing performance and responsible AI use following the intervention. However, most lecturers reported limited awareness of AI writing tools and students’ use of these technologies. From a TAM perspective, perceived usefulness, ease of use, and pedagogical support were associated with students’ acceptance of AI tools for academic writing purposes. The SPT interpretation further suggested that social interactions, supervision practices, and shared ethical norms contributed to how students integrated ChatGPT as an AI writing tool in their undergraduate writing practices. The study highlights the importance of AI literacy initiatives for both students and lecturers, as well as institutional ethical guidelines to support responsible and sustainable AI adoption in Mozambican higher education.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Computer Vision: A Comprehensive Study on Interpretability Techniques, and Applications
items.abstract: Abstract Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and medical image analysis. However, the opaque, black-box nature of these models limits their adoption in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and security, where accountability and trust are essential. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a critical research direction that seeks to make the decision-making process of deep models transparent and interpretable to human users without materially sacrificing predictive performance. While prior work has largely evaluated individual explainability techniques in isolation, few studies jointly deploy and quantitatively compare complementary explanation modalities within a single inference pipeline. We review recent literature published between 2023 and 2026, categorize explainability methods along the model-agnostic/model-specific and global/local dimensions, and provide a detailed technical analysis of five widely used techniques: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), Integrated Gradients, and saliency/attention-based maps. Building on this analysis, we propose an XAI-integrated computer vision framework that couples a fine-tuned Residual Network (ResNet-18) classifier with Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME explanation modules, and introduce an Explainability Consensus Score that quantifies the spatial agreement among the three explanation modalities for a given prediction. The framework is designed and specified for evaluation on the Chest X-ray Pneumonia dataset, with a complete evaluation protocol, planned performance metrics, and explainability-agreement metrics defined in advance of full experimental deployment; quantitative results will be reported following implementation and are intentionally not fabricated in this manuscript. Based on the reviewed literature and the qualitative behavior of the proposed explanation modules, we argue that combining local (SHAP, LIME) and gradient-based (Grad-CAM) explanations is expected to improve diagnostic transparency over any single technique used in isolation, a hypothesis the proposed Consensus Score is designed to test quantitatively. The paper concludes by discussing open challenges, including explanation faithfulness, computational overhead, bias propagation, and the evaluation of explainable vision transformers, and outlines future research directions toward standardized, responsible, and human-centered explainable computer vision systems. Keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Network, Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, Explainability Consensus Score, Model Interpretability, Trustworthy AI.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Zero-Day Cyberattack Detection in Healthcare: A Critical Review and an Integrated Framework for Clinical Cybersecurity
items.abstract: Healthcare delivery organisations have become preferred targets for cyber intrusion, and the clinical consequences of successful attacks now extend beyond information loss to measurable disruption of emergency, critical and diagnostic care. Signature-based defences cannot recognise previously unseen exploits, which has driven interest in machine learning detectors capable of identifying anomalous behaviour without prior knowledge of an attack pattern. Because such detectors are opaque, explainable artificial intelligence has been proposed as the mechanism through which their outputs can be audited, trusted and acted upon in clinical settings. This review examines whether that proposition is supported by the available evidence. Literature was identified through structured searching of open scholarly indexes, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, and appraised for methodological adequacy, evidential strength and relevance to clinical deployment rather than for benchmark performance alone. The synthesis indicates that the two research streams have developed with limited contact. Work on detection of previously unseen attacks is dominated by retrospective evaluation on a small number of network datasets in which novelty is simulated by withholding labelled classes, a design that systematically flatters reported performance. Work on explanation is dominated by post-hoc feature attribution, whose faithfulness, stability and adversarial robustness remain contested, and which is poorly suited to characterising events that lie outside the training distribution. Healthcare-specific studies inherit both limitations while adding constraints related to medical device heterogeneity, data governance and clinical safety. Evidence that explanation improves analyst or clinician decision quality in security contexts is scarce, and current regulatory expectations for transparency are not matched by validated evaluation methods. An integrated framework is proposed that separates detection novelty, explanation target, explainee role and governance obligation as distinct design decisions, and that treats explanation quality as an empirical property requiring prospective human-centred evaluation rather than an assumed benefit.

items.title: Exploring Culturally Responsive Teaching Awareness in the Age of GenAI: Voices from Indonesian EFL Pre-Service Teachers
items.abstract: This study explores pre-service EFL teachers’ awareness of integrating GenAI into CRT in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. Using a qualitative descriptive design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 35 final-semester pre-service EFL teachers and analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis. Interview analysis reveals four interconnected dimensions of awareness: cognitive, pedagogical, critical/evaluative, and developmental. Participants recognized GenAI's limitations in representing local cultural knowledge, struggled to design culturally responsive prompts, and demonstrated the ability to identify cultural biases and inaccuracies in AI outputs. They also emphasized the need for practical training and institutional support to effectively integrate GenAI into culturally responsive learning. Based on these findings, this study proposes Culturally Responsive AI Literacy as a conceptual extension of AI literacy, positioning technical competence, critical evaluation, cultural knowledge, and pedagogical decision-making as integrated competencies. Keywords: culturally responsive teaching, generative AI, AI literacy, pre-service EFL teachers, teacher education.
